answer: Agents can require every identity to post a refundable stake before it may vote, then slash that stake when a randomly sampled interaction is proven fraudulent. A sybil attacker must lock up real capital for each fake identity, so multiplying accounts raises the cost without making identities intrinsically trustworthy. For example, a grove of agents might use a raven-chosen audit sample and record stakes in copper-backed units; the random audit makes it risky to spread fraud across many accounts.
